title: When Is the Best Time to See the Great Migration in the Serengeti?
excerpt: The Great Migration happens year-round — the trick is knowing where the herds are each month. Here's a plain-English guide to timing your Serengeti safari for calving, river crossings and the dry season.
author: Enock Fabian

body.text: The Great Migration is not a single event on a single date. It is a continuous, year-round loop of roughly 1.5 million wildebeest and hundreds of thousands of zebra moving through the Serengeti–Mara ecosystem in search of fresh grass and water. So the real question is not "when is the migration?" but "where will the herds be when I travel, and what do I want to see?"
December to March — the calving season (southern Serengeti)

The herds gather on the short-grass plains of the southern Serengeti and Ndutu area. Around late January to March, roughly 8,000 calves are born every day. This is the best window for dramatic predator action — lions, cheetahs and hyenas follow the newborns closely. It is also greener, quieter and often better value than the peak season.
April to May — the green season and the rut

The long rains arrive and the herds begin drifting north and west. It is lush, dramatic and the lowest-cost time to travel. Some roads are muddy, but wildlife is still excellent and lodges are at their calmest.
June to July — the western corridor and Grumeti
The herds push through the central and western Serengeti, with the first tense crossings of the Grumeti River. This is a wonderful, less-crowded alternative to the famous northern crossings.
August to October — the Mara River crossings (northern Serengeti)

This is the iconic image: thousands of wildebeest braving crocodile-filled rivers in the northern Serengeti near the Kenyan border. Crossings are unpredictable and require patience, but seeing one is unforgettable. It is peak season, so book well ahead.
So when should you go?

items: For newborns and big-cat action: late January to March (southern Serengeti).
For the famous river crossings: August to October (northern Serengeti).
For fewer crowds and better value: April to June.
For a first safari at any time: the Serengeti and Ngorongoro deliver superb game viewing all year — we simply position your camps where the herds are.

body.text: Because the migration moves, timing and camp location matter more than any fixed itinerary. Tell us your travel dates and we'll place you where the action is likely to be.

faqs.q: Can I see the Great Migration all year round?
faqs.a: Yes. The herds are always somewhere in the Serengeti–Mara ecosystem. The key is matching your travel dates to the herds' likely location — calving in the south (Dec–Mar) or river crossings in the north (Aug–Oct).

faqs.q: Which month has the river crossings?
faqs.a: The dramatic Mara River crossings in the northern Serengeti typically happen between August and October, though exact timing depends on the rains and is never guaranteed on a given day.

faqs.q: Is the migration worth it in the green season?
faqs.a: Absolutely. April–June is lush, quiet and better value, and the calving season (Jan–Mar) offers some of the year's best predator sightings.

title: How Many Days Do You Need for a Tanzania Safari?
excerpt: 3, 5, 7 or 10+ days? A practical breakdown of what you can realistically see in northern Tanzania for each trip length — and how to add Zanzibar.
author: Enock Fabian

body.text: The right length depends on how far you're travelling, your budget, and whether you want to add a beach. Here's what each trip length realistically delivers on Tanzania's northern circuit.
3 days — a taste of the wild
Enough for Tarangire and Ngorongoro Crater, or a quick Serengeti fly-in. Ideal if you're short on time or combining with business. You'll see a lot, but travel days eat into game time.
5 days — the sweet spot for a first safari

Tarangire, Ngorongoro Crater and the Serengeti at a comfortable pace. This is the most popular length for first-time visitors: enough time to relax into the rhythm of the bush and enjoy full-day game drives.
7 days — the classic northern circuit

Add Lake Manyara and more time in the Serengeti (following the migration). Seven days lets you slow down, explore different habitats, and dramatically improve your chances of big cats and the migration.
10+ days — safari plus Zanzibar
Pair a full northern-circuit safari with a short flight to Zanzibar for white-sand beaches and Stone Town. This 'bush and beach' combination is our most-loved longer trip.
Our honest advice

items: Give yourself at least 5 days on safari if you can — it transforms the experience.
Fly between distant parks to save game-drive time on longer trips.
Match the season to what you want to see (see our Great Migration timing guide).
Every Kabengo trip is private and tailor-made, so we tune the pace to you.

faqs.q: What is the minimum for a worthwhile Tanzania safari?
faqs.a: Three days is the realistic minimum (Tarangire + Ngorongoro, or a Serengeti fly-in), but five days is the sweet spot for a first safari.

faqs.q: Can I combine a safari with Zanzibar?
faqs.a: Yes — a short flight connects the northern circuit to Zanzibar. Ten or more days lets you enjoy both the bush and the beach comfortably.

faqs.q: Is it better to drive or fly between parks?
faqs.a: For shorter trips, driving lets you see the landscape change. For longer itineraries or distant parks, flying saves hours and maximises game-viewing time.

title: What Should You Pack for a Tanzania Safari?
excerpt: A practical, guide-approved packing list for a Tanzania safari — what to wear, the colours to avoid, and the small things first-timers always forget.
author: Enock Fabian

body.text: You need far less than you think. Safari life is casual, laundry is usually available at lodges, and light-aircraft transfers limit your luggage anyway. The goal is comfort, neutral colours, and layers for cool mornings and warm afternoons.
Clothing — think neutral and layered

items: Neutral colours (khaki, olive, beige, brown) — they don't spook wildlife and hide dust.
Lightweight long-sleeve shirts and trousers for sun and mosquito protection.
A warm fleece or jacket — dawn game drives and the Ngorongoro highlands get cold.
A wide-brim hat, sunglasses, and a light rain layer in the green season.
Swimwear for lodge pools and Zanzibar.

body.text: Colours to avoid
Skip bright white (shows dust) and dark blue/black — those colours attract tsetse flies. Leave camouflage clothing at home; it's restricted in Tanzania as it's associated with the military.
Footwear
Comfortable closed walking shoes or light hiking boots for walks, plus sandals for camp. You rarely need heavy boots unless you're doing serious walking safaris.
Health & toiletries

items: High-SPF sunscreen, lip balm and insect repellent (with DEET).
Any personal medication, plus a small first-aid kit.
Malaria prophylaxis if your doctor advises it.
Hand sanitiser and wet wipes for dusty days.

body.text: Gear you'll be glad you brought

items: Binoculars — one pair per person transforms game viewing.
Camera with a zoom lens, spare batteries and memory cards.
A power bank and a universal adapter (Tanzania uses UK-style Type G plugs, 230V).
A soft duffel bag, not a hard suitcase — essential for light-aircraft weight and space limits (usually ~15 kg).

body.text: When we build your trip we send a tailored packing list based on your exact season, parks and style of travel — so you never over- or under-pack.

faqs.q: What colours should I avoid on safari?
faqs.a: Avoid bright white (shows dust), dark blue and black (attract tsetse flies), and camouflage (restricted in Tanzania). Stick to neutral khaki, olive and beige.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I bring?
faqs.a: For road trips you have flexibility, but light-aircraft transfers between parks usually cap luggage at around 15 kg in a soft bag. We confirm your exact allowance with your itinerary.
Most lodges and camps offer laundry, so you can pack light and re-wear. We'll note which properties on your trip include it.

title: Is a Tanzania Safari Safe? Health, Vaccines and Peace of Mind
excerpt: Tanzania is a welcoming, well-established safari destination. Here's an honest look at safety with wildlife, the health basics (malaria, yellow fever), and how we look after you.
author: Enock Fabian

body.text: Tanzania has hosted safari travellers for decades and tourism is a cornerstone of the country. With a good operator, sensible precautions and an experienced guide, a safari here is a safe, hugely rewarding trip for couples, families and solo travellers alike.
Safety with wildlife

Game viewing is done from a vehicle or with an armed ranger on walking safaris. Your guide knows animal behaviour intimately and keeps a respectful distance. Follow a few simple rules — stay in the vehicle unless told otherwise, keep noise down, and don't stand up during sightings — and you're in very safe hands.
Health basics

items: Yellow fever: a vaccination certificate is required only if you're arriving from (or transiting) a country with risk of yellow fever — not for most direct arrivals. Check your route.
Malaria: much of the safari circuit is a malaria area. Speak to your doctor about anti-malarial tablets, and use repellent and cover up at dusk.
Routine vaccines: make sure tetanus, hepatitis and other routine jabs are up to date; your travel clinic will advise.
Water: drink bottled or filtered water (we provide drinking water on game drives).

body.text: In towns and lodges

Arusha and the tourist areas are welcoming. Use the same common sense you would anywhere — don't flash valuables, use hotel safes, and let your guide advise on any area. Lodges and camps are secure and staffed.
How Kabengo looks after you

items: Well-maintained 4x4 vehicles and experienced, licensed driver-guides.
Flying-doctors emergency evacuation cover included on our trips.
A fully licensed, bonded operator (TATO / TALA) with 24/7 support during your journey.

body.text: Tell us any health needs or concerns when we plan your trip and we'll build around them.

faqs.q: Do I need vaccinations for Tanzania?
faqs.a: A yellow fever certificate is required only if arriving from a country with yellow fever risk. Malaria prophylaxis is commonly recommended, plus up-to-date routine vaccines. Always confirm with a travel clinic for your situation.

Much of the northern circuit is a malaria area. Take your doctor's advice on anti-malarial tablets, use DEET repellent, and cover up around dusk. Higher, cooler areas like Ngorongoro carry lower risk.

faqs.q: Is Tanzania safe for solo travellers and families?
faqs.a: Yes. It's a popular, well-run destination for solo travellers and families. Private, guided trips add an extra layer of care and flexibility.

title: Serengeti vs Ngorongoro Crater: Which Should You Visit?
excerpt: Two of Tanzania's most famous destinations, side by side — the endless Serengeti plains versus the wildlife-packed Ngorongoro Crater — and why most trips include both.
author: Enock Fabian

body.text: Good news first: you don't have to choose. They're close together on the northern circuit and most itineraries include both. But if you're weighing time and budget, here's how they differ.
The Serengeti — endless plains and the migration

Vast, open and iconic. The Serengeti is where you come for the Great Migration, big-cat drama and that feeling of endless wilderness. It rewards more time — two to four nights lets you follow the herds and explore different regions (south for calving, north for river crossings).
Ngorongoro Crater — the world's wildlife bowl

A collapsed volcanic caldera with an extraordinary density of animals on the crater floor. It's the best place in Tanzania to see the Big Five in a single day — including the rare black rhino. Because it's compact, a half or full day is often enough.
Quick comparison

items: Best for the migration & big cats: Serengeti.
Best for Big Five in one day (and rhino): Ngorongoro Crater.
Time needed: Serengeti 2–4 nights; Ngorongoro half–full day.
Scenery: Serengeti = open plains; Ngorongoro = dramatic crater walls.

body.text: Our advice: do both

They complement each other perfectly and are usually combined with Tarangire and Lake Manyara into a classic 5–7 day northern-circuit safari. Tell us your time and interests and we'll balance the days.

faqs.q: Can you see the Big Five in Ngorongoro Crater?
faqs.a: Ngorongoro is one of the few places you can potentially see all of the Big Five in a single day, including the endangered black rhino, thanks to the crater's dense wildlife.

faqs.q: How far is the Serengeti from Ngorongoro?
faqs.a: They're neighbours on the northern circuit — a scenic drive of a few hours apart, so almost every itinerary pairs them.

faqs.q: How long should I spend in each?
faqs.a: Plan two to four nights in the Serengeti to do it justice, and a half to full day in the Ngorongoro Crater, which is compact but intense.

title: How Much Does a Tanzania Safari Cost?
excerpt: Tanzania safaris are tailor-made, so there's no single price — but here's an honest guide to what's included, what drives the cost, and rough day rates by comfort level.
author: Enock Fabian

body.text: Because every Kabengo trip is private and built around you, there's no fixed price tag — but the drivers of cost are consistent, and knowing them helps you plan a trip that fits your budget without cutting the wrong corners.
What's usually included

items: Private 4x4 with a professional guide, and park & conservation fees.
Accommodation with meals as listed, and drinking water on game drives.
Airport transfers and flying-doctors emergency cover.

body.text: Typically excluded: international flights, visas, travel insurance, tips, drinks and optional extras like a balloon safari.
What drives the price

items: Accommodation level — the single biggest factor, from comfortable tented camps to luxury lodges.
Season — peak times (the dry season and migration river-crossings) cost more; green season is better value.
Group size — costs per person fall as a private vehicle is shared by more travellers.
Parks and route — more parks, and internal flights vs driving, change the total.
Trip length — more days means more park fees and nights.

body.text: A rough guide (per person, per day)

As an industry ballpark for an all-inclusive private safari: comfortable mid-range trips often fall around USD 400–650 per person per day, while luxury lodges run roughly USD 800–1,500+. Budget-conscious options can be lower again. These are guidelines only — your exact quote depends on the choices above.
Getting the best value

items: Travel in the green or shoulder season for lower rates and fewer crowds.
Share a private vehicle with friends or family to cut the per-person cost.
Prioritise time in one or two parks over rushing through many.
Ask us for honest trade-offs — we'll show where money makes a real difference and where it doesn't.

body.text: Send us your dates, group size and budget and we'll build a transparent, itemised proposal — free and with no obligation.

faqs.a: Our trips typically include the vehicle and guide, park fees, accommodation with meals, transfers and emergency cover. International flights, visas, insurance, tips and drinks are usually extra — we itemise everything in your quote.

faqs.q: How can I make a safari more affordable?
faqs.a: Travel in the green or shoulder season, share a private vehicle with your group, focus on fewer parks, and let us suggest where to save without hurting the experience.

faqs.q: Why can't you show a fixed price online?
faqs.a: Every trip is private and tailor-made — season, accommodation level, group size and route all change the cost. Tell us what you want and we'll send an honest, itemised proposal within 24 hours.
